Custom managers own their caching semantics and must preserve presence separately from null/default values. Generated
synchronous methods use the underlying implementation directly when a custom manager has no internal sync capability.

## Reading without loading

```cs
var lookup = await cache.TryGetAsync<Order>("order:42");
if (lookup.Found)
{
    Console.WriteLine(lookup.Value);
}
```

`TryGetAsync` takes the same `version` an entry was stored with.

## Versions and the stored key

An entry stored with `WithVersion` lives under a different key than the unversioned one: `entry` at version 1 never
shares a value with the key `entry::v1`. Keys that begin with a NUL character are escaped too. `TryGetAsync` and `InvalidateKeysAsync` accept that same logical key and optional
version; they apply the same framing as storage. `InvalidateKeyAsync(key, version)` is a convenience for one logical key.
`ICacheAdministrator` takes the stored key, `MethodCacheKeys.StoredKey(key, version)`, which is what
`CacheEntryInfo.StoredKey` shows; treat its format as opaque. To invalidate a versioned entry through `ICacheManager`,
pass the key and its version, `InvalidateKeyAsync(key, version: 2)`, not the stored key.

## Many keys at once

Key, tag and clear invalidation also guard the batch factory while it reads its source. Its caller can receive the in-flight result, but invalidated candidates are not published into memory or the distributed cache. Individual callers can still load and publish these keys during the batch; a fresh concurrent value wins.

`GetOrCreateManyAsync` checks the local cache for every key, looks up the local misses in the distributed cache,
and calls the factory once with the keys neither holds. Each key gets the value the cache selects: memory first, then
the distributed cache, then the factory. A bulk read therefore agrees with individual reads of the same keys, even
across nodes: a value another node stored in the distributed cache is returned as is, and its key is not passed to
the factory. A concurrent writer may still win over a value the factory produced; the returned dictionary then holds
the writer's value, as an individual read would:

```cs
var users = await cache.GetOrCreateManyAsync<User>(
    userIds.Select(id => $"user:{id}"),
    async (missingKeys, ct) =>
    {
        var ids = missingKeys.Select(k => int.Parse(k["user:".Length..])).ToList();
        var loaded = await repository.GetUsersAsync(ids, ct);   // one query for all misses
        return loaded.ToDictionary(u => $"user:{u.Id}", u => u);
    },
    o => o.WithDuration(TimeSpan.FromHours(1)));
```

- The factory returns an `IReadOnlyDictionary` with a value for each key it gets, and the call returns one for every
  key.
- On a hot path, build the options once and pass the `CacheEntryOptions` instead of a builder action.
- Each key behaves as `GetOrCreateAsync` would for it. When the factory throws, each key it was asked for gets its
  fail-safe value; when a key has none, the factory's exception is thrown.
- `cancellationToken` stops this caller's wait. A factory that ignores it finishes in the background, and its values
  are cached unless they were invalidated while it ran.

## Things to know

- Concurrent calls for the same key share one factory run. A caller's `cancellationToken` stops its own wait; if it
  cancels a run others joined, they run the factory again rather than fail.
- A factory that asks for the key it is loading (itself, or through the cached service it belongs to) would wait for
  itself, so that call throws an `InvalidOperationException` instead, and the key is free for the next caller.
- To cache a sequence, materialize it in the factory (`await query.ToListAsync(ct)`) and cache the list.
- The four operations on `ICacheManager` can be mocked directly. The options-builder convenience overload
  delegates to that interface. You can also pass a `NoOpCacheManager` ([Testing](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/testing.md)).

Manual `TryGetAsync` reads a fresh entry, including a cached null, even when refresh-ahead is due. This lookup does not start a factory or background refresh.

Caller cancellation stops the wait during an L2 read or a slow factory, including bulk reads and fail-safe waits. Shared work may finish for other callers; cancellation is not reported as a dependency failure.


---

<!-- source: docs/features/third-party.md -->

# Caching third-party code

MethodCache can cache calls to code you don't own, such as API clients, cloud SDKs or payment gateways, to cut API
costs and latency. Pick one of three approaches:

| Approach | Best for |
|----------|----------|
| `[assembly: CacheInterface]` | A client that ships an interface: cache chosen methods with one line, no wrapper |
| A wrapper interface with `[Cache]` | A client without an interface (a sealed class or static methods) |
| `ICacheManager.GetOrCreateAsync` | One or two calls, or keys you want to build yourself |

## The client's own interface

Name the interface and the methods to cache in an assembly attribute, anywhere in your project:

```cs
[assembly: CacheInterface(typeof(IFxRatesClient), nameof(IFxRatesClient.GetRateAsync),
    Duration = "00:01:00", Tags = ["fx", "fx:{from}"])]
```

```cs
builder.Services.AddSingleton<IFxRatesClient, FxRatesClient>();   // the vendor's client, registered as usual
builder.Services.AddMethodCache();
```

- The listed methods behave like methods with `[Cache]`: keys from the arguments, tag templates with the method's
  parameter names, zero-allocation hits on .NET 10. Methods you don't list always reach the client, so writes
  are never cached by accident.
- The attribute's settings (`Duration`, `Tags`, `Group`, `SlidingExpiration`, `RefreshAhead`, `Version`, `FailSafe`,
  `FailSafeTimeout`, `FailSafeRetryAfter`, `Enabled`, `Distributed`) apply to every listed method. Give one method its
  own settings like any cached method:

```cs
builder.Services.AddMethodCache(config => config.Method((IFxRatesClient c) => c.GetRateAsync(Any<string>.Value, Any<string>.Value))
    .Configure(o => o.WithDuration(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30))));
```

- The method id in `appsettings.json` and the admin endpoints is the name of the assembly that declares the interface
  (the vendor's, not yours) in brackets, the interface's full name, a dot and the method name, for example
  `[FxVendor]FxVendor.IFxRatesClient.GetRateAsync`. `IMethodCacheKeys.MethodId` returns it for you.
- List each interface once. It must be non-generic and come from another assembly; for your own interfaces, put
  `[Cache]` on the methods. A method with overloads can't be listed yet.
- The attribute can live in a class library, such as your infrastructure project. Select its generated module
  explicitly with `MethodCacheBuilder.FromAssemblyOf<T>()`, using a type declared in that assembly. This also
  bootstraps the module under Native AOT without relying on discovery of loaded assemblies.
- When multiple assemblies generate the same interface, select exactly one module. Calling and entry assemblies
  have no special precedence. An ambiguous registration throws `InvalidOperationException` naming the candidates.

```cs
builder.Services.AddMethodCache(cache => cache.FromAssemblyOf<Rates>());
```

- Mistakes are build errors: [MC0011](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/user-guide/DIAGNOSTICS.md#mc0011) (a type it can't cache, such as one with
  static abstract or non-public abstract members), [MC0012](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/user-guide/DIAGNOSTICS.md#mc0012) (a method that is
  missing, overloaded, static, or one `[Cache]` would reject) and [MC0013](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/user-guide/DIAGNOSTICS.md#mc0013) (an
  interface listed twice).

## A wrapper interface

Define an interface in your project with the calls you need, and put the settings on it:

```cs
public interface IRates
{
    [Cache(Duration = "00:01:00", Tags = ["fx", "fx:{from}"])]
    Task<decimal> GetAsync(string from, string to);
}

public sealed class Rates(FxRatesClient client) : IRates   // calls the vendor's concrete class
{
    public Task<decimal> GetAsync(string from, string to) => client.GetRateAsync(from, to);
}
```

```cs
builder.Services.AddSingleton<FxRatesClient>();
builder.Services.AddScoped<IRates, Rates>();
builder.Services.AddMethodCache();
```

Static methods and sealed classes work the same way: the wrapper calls them, and the interface carries the attributes.

## An explicit key

```cs
var rate = await cache.GetOrCreateAsync(
    $"fx:{from}:{to}",
    async ct => await client.GetRateAsync(from, to),
    o => o.WithDuration(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(1)).AddTags("fx"));
```

See [Manual caching](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/manual-caching.md).

## Things to know

- **Leave writes uncached.** Payments, uploads and deletes must not be cached; mark wrapper methods that change data
  with `[CacheInvalidate(Tags = ...)]`.
- **Exceptions are not cached.** With [fail-safe](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/fail-safe.md) on, the previous value is served while the client
  fails.
- **Invalidate from a webhook** with `cache.InvalidateTagAsync("fx:EUR")` when the vendor tells you data changed.
- **Share results between instances** with a [distributed cache](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/distributed-cache.md) when every instance calls the
  same paid API.
- **Start with short durations** and lengthen them once you know how fresh the data must be.


---

<!-- source: docs/features/http-caching.md -->

# HTTP response caching

Add `AddHttpCaching()` to an `HttpClient` registration to cache HTTP responses according to their response headers,
as RFC 9111 describes. Freshness comes from `Cache-Control` and expiry headers; `ETag` and `Last-Modified` enable
conditional validation, and a successful 304 is returned to the caller as the full response.

Chapter 11 of the [console tour](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/samples/MethodCache.Demo#httpclient-caching) starts a local HTTP server and checks cache hits, ETag/304 validation, `no-store` and invalidation after PUT. It needs no external API or Docker.

```cs
builder.Services.AddMethodCache();
builder.Services.AddHttpClient<IGitHubClient, GitHubClient>()
    .AddHttpCaching();
```

The [package guide](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/src/MethodCache.HttpCaching/README.md) covers settings, storage, private and shared caches,
limits and metrics. This page covers the rules the cache follows and Core-owned storage. See
[Security](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/security.md#methodcachehttpcaching) for the threat model.

Responses without custom key headers or `Vary` fields use direct variant selection, avoiding temporary sets
and sorting. Private caches still isolate `Authorization` and `Cookie`; configured headers and `Vary` retain
their combined, case-insensitive selection rules.

A full replacement response also retires the previous cached representation when it cannot be stored, including `no-store`, shared-cache `private`, a body over the size limit, or a failed replacement write. The next caller cannot fall back to an older fresh body. Stale-while-revalidate respects explicit request `max-age`, `min-fresh` and `max-stale` limits.

Concurrent writers with the same variant selection share its namespace, including across processes using distributed storage. The body-free variant index is retained for the maximum supported response lifetime (365 days); individual variants still expire at their own TTL. A change to the selecting headers retires the URL publication epoch exactly once; a concurrent response published after that retirement remains reachable; the current response reaches its caller, and the next request fetches and stores the new schema. If deleting the old entry fails after the epoch was rotated, foreground validation reports that error without rotating again; background validation logs it. A concurrent publication in the new epoch remains reachable.

## Freshness and validation

- Stale-while-revalidate and stale-if-error are optional. Response `no-cache` requires successful validation before
  the response is reused, even when either option is on. Request `no-cache` has the same requirement: a 5xx response
  or network error reaches the caller rather than falling back to cached content.
- `must-revalidate` forbids serving a stale response, as do `proxy-revalidate` and `s-maxage` in a shared cache.
- An `Expires` at or before the response `Date`, or one that doesn't parse (such as `Expires: 0`), makes the response
  stale at once. Heuristic freshness and `DefaultMaxAge` don't extend it. An explicit `max-age` (or `s-maxage` in a
  shared cache) wins over `Expires`.
- A 304 updates the stored response's headers and whether it may be stored. If it changes to `no-store`, `Vary: *`, or
  `private` in a shared cache, the stored response is removed. This applies to background revalidation too. A 304
  without `Vary` keeps the original variant selection. If the updated response can't be stored, the old one is
  removed so its old rules are never used again; the caller still gets the response. If removing it fails too, the
  error reaches the caller.
- A `Cache-Control` or `Vary` field that doesn't parse (such as `private; max-age=600` or `max-age=-1`), also next to a valid one, is not
  read as absent: the response is not stored, because the header may have said `private` or `no-store`.
- An entry is kept at most a year, even when `Expires` is far in the future (`31 Dec 9999`).
- Weak ETags (`W/"abc"`) are sent back as weak validators.
- `only-if-cached` never contacts the origin, including for range requests, requests with their own validators,
  `no-store`, methods that aren't cached and background revalidation. When no stored response can be used, the
  answer is 504.

## Redirects, retries and request bodies

- A redirect the transport follows (`AllowAutoRedirect`, the default) answers a different URL, so it is not stored
  under the URL you requested. The transport also drops `Authorization` on a redirect, so storing it could hand one
  caller's response to another. Requests that end at the redirect target are cached under that URL as usual. If the
  target answers the cache's own validators with 304, the request is sent again without them, so you get the full response.
  A URL that was cached and now redirects has its stored response removed, also when background revalidation finds out.
- The cache stores responses for the request as you sent it, before the transport adds headers such as
  `Accept-Encoding` for automatic decompression. `Vary: Accept-Encoding` therefore works with `AutomaticDecompression`.
- The `If-None-Match` / `If-Modified-Since` headers the cache adds are removed again before the response is
  returned, so a retry handler (Polly, standard resilience) that sends the same message again gets a full response.
- A `GET` or `HEAD` with a body (search APIs such as Elasticsearch) goes to the origin: its URL doesn't identify it.
- The URL fragment (`#top`) is not part of the key; it never reaches the origin.

## Writes and invalidation

A successful `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH` or `DELETE` starts a new cache generation for its URL before it returns. That is
the URL you sent it to, also when the response redirects (`303 See Other`) elsewhere. A GET or
background revalidation that was already in flight can still complete, but it stores its response under the old
generation, so later requests fetch the updated response. With native Redis or SQL Server configured, the generation is shared by every instance, even when backplane
messages are lost. One bounded metadata batch captures the global, URL, client and static-tag generations before origin work.
SQL Server reads already initialized, permanent generation records without rewriting them. Missing or
non-permanent records are still initialized or repaired atomically; every lookup reads shared storage.
The transport retains only its latest bounded command-text shape. It does not cache generation values;
reordered or duplicate keys still return generations in the caller's order.

The built-in storage groups URLs into 4096 generation slots per storage prefix, so its metadata stays bounded. Two
URLs that share a slot can cause an extra cache miss when either is invalidated. Local invalidation also removes
the retired bodies from that slot, releasing their byte budget immediately. Generation records never expire on
their own; if the backend evicts one anyway, the next request starts a new generation, so a lost record only causes
cache misses and never brings back a response from before a write. If reading the generation fails, the request goes
to the origin. If advancing a generation cannot be confirmed, `HttpCacheInvalidationException` reaches the caller and Core retains
bounded recovery. The origin mutation may have succeeded: do not automatically retry it. A GET or HEAD whose answer
replaces a stored response that can't be retired throws the same exception; it is safe to retry. Cancelling the caller stops
its wait, while owned generation recovery continues. Graceful asynchronous disposal waits for owned advances, then
tries queued URL invalidations once more even while the circuit breaker is open. Each transport operation remains
bounded by its configured timeout. Any invalidations still unconfirmed at shutdown are reported as a count and are
lost when the process exits; other nodes may retain old responses until they expire.

## Core storage and administration

`AddHttpCaching` requires an explicit `AddMethodCache` registration in the same container. Either registration
order works. Without L2, Core uses a separate HTTP byte budget (100 MiB by default), independent of method entries.
Bodies exceeding the whole HTTP budget remain streamed and are not stored. Headers and metadata are charged too.
With MethodCache Redis or SQL Server configured, HTTP responses live exclusively in that owned L2; the application's
unrelated `IDistributedCache` is never a fallback. HTTP entries use an internal codec, independent of method serializers.
The former `HttpCacheStorageOptions`, `IHttpCacheStorage` and `HttpCacheEntry` public extension points are removed.

`ICacheAdministrator` lists actual local representations, or at most 1024 historical local L2 observations.
`Storage=ObservedDistributed` is not verified backend presence or a global inventory; observations contain no body,
credentials, cookie header or raw URL query. An unknown observation id returns NotFound. Removing a known id retires
its URL generation and all variants. `Clear` retires the shared global generation. Client tags are
`http:` followed by `MethodCacheKeys.Part(clientName)`; configured static `HttpCacheOptions.Tags` participate too.
The HTTP administration and byte statistics also work with a NoOp method manager.

Local client-tag invalidation scans resident HTTP entries and reclaims matching bodies and their byte budget.
Its work grows with the resident entry count; URL invalidation and other configured application tags use their indexes.
This keeps the implicit client tag out of the publication index while preserving administration and generation checks.

## Transport and cookies

`AddHttpCaching()` turns off automatic cookies on the client's `SocketsHttpHandler` or `HttpClientHandler`, after all
other configuration of that handler, so the default registration caches at once. Other named clients are unaffected.
A handler that already has cookies off is left alone, so a cookie-free handler shared between clients keeps working.
`ConfigureHttpClientDefaults(b => b.AddHttpCaching())` caches every client, each under its own name: two clients
never share entries, and they all use the settings given there. A client has at most one cache: calling
`AddHttpCaching` again for one client, or twice, adds no second cache and applies every settings delegate. To give
one client other settings, use `services.Configure<HttpCacheOptions>("name", o => ...)`.
`KeepCookies=true` preserves the transport configuration and completely bypasses response caching, validation and
stale fallback. `only-if-cached` then returns 504. A successful unsafe mutation still retires shared generations.
Send caller cookies as request headers; a handler that keeps a hidden cookie jar belongs on a client without HTTP
caching.

The cache runs after every other handler you add, so caller identity and rewritten requests are visible before
lookup.

Other transports (wrappers the cache can't see into, native platform handlers), and handlers inside the primary
transport or below a cache handler you construct yourself, can't be checked. They bypass caching and log one warning
per named client, unless you set `AllowUnverifiedTransport`. Set it only when you have checked that the whole
transport sends no automatic cookies or hidden caller identity. A known transport with automatic cookies turned on
always bypasses.

HTTP cache freshness includes request/response delay when correcting the upstream Age header, for both initial responses and 304 validation. Age arithmetic saturates instead of overflowing on extreme headers.

Background HTTP revalidation preserves the request HTTP version, version policy and a shallow copy of its request options. Option values keep their original ownership; use values that remain valid for background work.


---

<!-- source: docs/features/distributed-cache.md -->

# Distributed cache

The [web demo](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/samples/MethodCache.WebDemo) includes two-instance request examples and automated
Redis outage/restart scenarios. Both hosts share a transactional SQLite database, and query counters distinguish
Redis hits from source reads. Its tests own their Redis container and never stop a developer's Redis.

By default each application instance has its own in-memory cache. Add a distributed cache to share results between
instances and keep them across restarts:

```cs
builder.Services.AddMethodCache(mc => mc.UseRedis("localhost:6379"));   // MethodCache.Redis
```

```cs
builder.Services.AddMethodCache(mc => mc.UseSqlServer(connectionString));   // MethodCache.SqlServer
```

Redis backplane publication stops waiting when its token is cancelled. A cancelled unsubscribe acknowledgement does not fail application shutdown. SQL backplane identity gaps are not forgotten just because a transaction took longer than five seconds: committed gap rows are read without waiting, and a separate `NOWAIT` locking probe confirms an older identity is absent before it is forgotten. A locked or timed-out probe leaves gaps available for retry while newer invalidations and other committed gap messages are delivered.

Redis backplane recovery retries transient unsubscribe/subscribe failures after reconnect, with a delay that doubles from one second to at most 30 seconds. It reports connected only after subscription acknowledgement and the local recovery clear; shutdown cancels pending retries.

## How it works

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A([Call a cached method]):::dark --> B{In memory?<br/>L1}
    B -- yes --> R([Return the value]):::amber
    B -- no --> C{In Redis or<br/>SQL Server? L2}
    C -- yes --> D[Keep it in memory]:::light --> R
    C -- no --> E[Run your method]:::dark --> F[Write it to L1 and L2]:::light --> R
    classDef dark fill:#1E1B3A,stroke:#1E1B3A,color:#F5F3FF
    classDef amber fill:#FFB020,stroke:#FFB020,color:#1E1B3A
    classDef light fill:#F5F3FF,stroke:#1E1B3A,color:#1E1B3A
```

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Instance A
    participant L2 as Redis / SQL Server
    participant B as Instance B
    A->>A: [CacheInvalidate] or InvalidateTagsAsync
    A->>L2: Remove the key, or stamp the tag
    A-->>B: Backplane message (pub/sub, or the next poll)
    B->>B: Drop the in-memory copy
    Note over B: The next call reads L2 or runs the method
```

- Results live in memory (L1) and in the distributed cache (L2). An in-memory miss reads the distributed cache before
  running your method, and a new result is written to both.
- Invalidating a key removes it from the distributed cache. Invalidating a tag records when it happened, so older
  entries with that tag read as misses. A backplane tells every other instance to drop its in-memory copy: at once
  with Redis pub/sub, or on their next poll (every second by default) with SQL Server.
- Only Redis and Microsoft SQL Server are supported. Other stores, such as PostgreSQL, are not; the storage
  interfaces are internal. Use one of them: `UseRedis` and `UseSqlServer` together throw. `Distributed(...)` and
  `UseMessagePack()` without either log a warning at startup, since they have nothing to apply to.
- `[Cache]` methods and `GetOrCreateAsync` need no changes.
- MethodCache keeps its own distributed cache and connection, so your application's `IDistributedCache` is left alone.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Run the same MethodCache version on every instance that shares a cache and backplane; messages from another version
> are ignored with one warning.

## Policy isolation

Declared methods with equal effective startup/configuration options share a stable L2 namespace. A behavior-changing
runtime override uses a private namespace for that method and container. Equal overrides on different nodes cannot
share private values. Removing an override invalidates the declared method before allowing shared L2 reads again.
The logical key from `MethodCacheKeys` remains suitable for invalidation across policy variants.

A received method invalidation retires data for all closed generic and keyed registrations, without changing the
receiver's policy. Dissemination is best effort: a missed message can leave remote L1 values until expiry or reconnect.
L2 metadata rejects values loaded before invalidation, including writes that land after a timeout and retry.

Entries retain load start, first publication time and an absolute deadline. L2 reads apply the receiver's null policy
and result predicate, and cap remaining lifetime by the stored deadline, its own duration from first publication and
`MaxExpiration`. A slow factory does not consume the value's duration; it reduces the remaining metadata-retention margin.
Synchronous methods currently use L1 and the origin when these providers cannot offer a bounded native synchronous
operation. This emits a diagnostic once per method/container. Synchronous invalidation retires local data immediately
and leaves L2 recovery owned by the cache.

## Invalidation results

`InvalidateKeysAsync` and `InvalidateTagsAsync` validate the full batch and count distinct targets. `Requested` and
`Local` count targets, including local no-ops. `Distributed` counts confirmed L2 metadata; `Queued` counts unconfirmed
L2 targets. With L2 configured, their sum equals `Requested`. `Published` counts backplane sends and
`PublicationQueued` counts confirmed L2 targets whose sends need retry. A send does not confirm receipt by every node.
There are no distributed counters without L2 and no publication counters without a backplane.

Cancellation before mutation leaves data untouched. Afterwards it cancels the caller's wait while owned recovery
continues. Storage and publication have separate bounded queues, exposed through administration and health checks.

## When the distributed cache is down

Calls keep working from memory and your methods; the distributed cache never fails or stalls a call. Each call to it
is capped at `OperationTimeout` (one second), a circuit breaker skips it until it is back, and invalidations are queued and retried
instead of throwing. Until they are stored, the instance doesn't read entries from it, so an invalidated value can't
come back. The [health check](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/monitoring.md#health-check) reports Degraded while this lasts.

Queued invalidations are stored a batch at a time once the cache answers, so a long outage's backlog drains at the
pace the cache can take. More than 10,000 are replaced by one clear of the distributed cache (logged as a warning),
and so is an invalidation the cache keeps refusing while it answers everything else, so neither holds up the rest.
The queue lives in memory: when the instance shuts down, it waits for writes still running, then tries once more to store
what is queued, each step (stamp, removal, publish) capped by `OperationTimeout`, and logs a warning with the number it had to drop. Other instances can read those invalidated
values from the distributed cache until they expire.

A value set directly while the distributed cache is down stays in that instance's memory, and the value it replaced is
removed from the distributed cache and the other instances once it is back. An entry that comes back damaged (cut
short, or unreadable by the serializer) is a miss: your method runs and its result replaces the entry.

The timeout caps each call to the distributed cache, not a whole cache miss. A cache that stops answering costs a miss
one timeout, after which the circuit breaker skips it. One that answers just within the timeout costs a miss up to
three: reading the entry, writing your method's result and checking that no removal raced the write (and a fourth for
the backplane message).

## Options

`DistributedCacheOptions` apply to the owned Redis and SQL Server providers:

```cs
builder.Services.AddMethodCache(mc => mc.Distributed(options =>
{
    options.OperationTimeout = TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(500);
    options.CircuitBreakerDuration = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30);
}));
```

| Option | Default | |
|---|---|---|
| `OperationTimeout` | 1 second | The longest one call to the distributed cache may take. A slower call is abandoned and counts as a failure, except a write (see [What other instances see](#what-other-instances-see)) |
| `CircuitBreakerDuration` | 10 seconds | How long the distributed cache is skipped after a failure or timeout. Invalidations it didn't accept are retried at this interval |
| `ClockSkewTolerance` | 2 seconds | How far apart your servers' clocks may be. A tag invalidation also applies to entries created up to this long after it. One stamped further ahead of an instance's clock (by a server whose clock runs fast) counts from when that instance first read it, until its clock reaches the stamp |
| `TagCheckInterval` | 1 second | How long an instance trusts the invalidation time it last read for a tag. Without a backplane, an entry read from the distributed cache can outlive a tag invalidation made on another instance by up to this long |
| `TagRetention` | 1 day | How long tag invalidations are kept. An entry stays in the distributed cache at most `TagRetention - ClockSkewTolerance` from when your method started loading it (less if its own duration is shorter); a load that takes longer is kept only in that instance's memory. Both values are truncated to whole milliseconds, and `TagRetention` must exceed `ClockSkewTolerance` by at least one millisecond, or startup fails; with SQL Server it must also end before 9999-12-31 |
| `KeyPrefix` | `methodcache:` | One startup-immutable prefix for values, metadata, HTTP epochs and the backplane; give each application its own |
| `VerifyRoundTrip` | `true` | Verify the serialized representation before publishing; not a proof of semantic equality |
| `SerializerVersion` | `1` | Positive value-format identity; increment when changing serializer settings |

## What other instances see

- An invalidation reaches another instance when the backplane delivers it. Until then, and for good if the message is
  lost or the instance is disconnected from the backplane, that instance serves its in-memory copy until it expires,
  as without a backplane. Instances without a copy read the distributed cache, which is already right.
- Messages carry no values, so a late, repeated or reordered message only makes an instance read the distributed cache
  again.
- An invalidation the distributed cache didn't accept is retried every `CircuitBreakerDuration`. Until the retry
  succeeds, other instances can serve the old value; the instance that invalidated never does.
- A write that timed out (a large value, say) doesn't open the circuit breaker, since the cache may answer everything
  else: the instance logs a warning and keeps using it. Such a write may still land later, because a distributed cache
  has no compare-and-set, so its key is removed again after `CircuitBreakerDuration` (as after a write that failed,
  once the cache answers). Further timed-out writes of the key push that one removal back, and an instance that shuts
  down first removes the key while it shuts down. Until then the late value can replace a newer one, and a write that
  lands after that removal stays until it expires.
- Entries carry no checksum: damage that still reads as a valid value is served.

## Serialization

Values are written as JSON with System.Text.Json, public fields included, so value tuples and structs with fields
are shared as they are. Every value an instance writes is read back and written again first; when that doesn't give
the same bytes and type, that value and every later value of the method with that type stay in the instance's memory
only, and one warning names the method and the type. Each value is checked, since one with default data (an `Id` of
0 behind a private setter) can come back unchanged where the next one doesn't. A serializer that never writes the same
bytes twice (encryption with a fresh nonce) can't be compared that way, so for it only the type is checked. State
the serializer never writes at all (a class that keeps its data only in private fields, which JSON writes as `{}`)
reads back as the same bytes, so the check can't see that it is lost: make such state serializable, or register a
serializer that writes it. That happens with properties that have a
private or protected setter, public readonly fields of a type that also has a parameterless constructor, a derived
type returned as its declared base type (an `Animal` method returning a `Dog`, even after it returned plain
`Animal`s), and `object`, with JSON and MessagePack alike. A value the serializer throws on (a cycle, a delegate
field) stays in memory the same way. A collection declared as an interface (`IReadOnlyList<int>`,
`IEnumerable<int>`) may come back as another implementation, a `List<int>` for an array, and is still shared. The
check looks at the type of the value itself, not of what it holds: a `Dog` inside a `List<Animal>` or in a property
declared `Animal` is shared without its `Dog` data. To share such values, register a serializer that reads them back,
through `UseJson` with your own `JsonSerializerOptions` or `JsonSerializerContext` (`[JsonInclude]` on the
setter, `[JsonDerivedType]` on the base type). The `MethodCache.Serialization.MessagePack` package makes values
smaller and faster to read:

```cs
builder.Services.AddMethodCache(mc => mc
    .UseRedis("localhost:6379")
    .UseMessagePack());   // MethodCache.Serialization.MessagePack
```

Entries written in the other format read as misses and are replaced, so switching needs no flush. See the
[MessagePack package guide](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/src/MethodCache.Serialization.MessagePack/README.md). Under Native AOT, register your
`JsonSerializerContext` ([Native AOT](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/native-aot.md)).

## Owned storage and compatibility

Use `MethodCacheBuilder.UseRedis` or `UseSqlServer`. Storage, backplane, atomic metadata and serializers are internal owned services; the application's `IDistributedCache` is never a fallback. Configure `DistributedCacheOptions.KeyPrefix` with `mc.Distributed(o => o.KeyPrefix = ...)` before building the container. All registrations participate, including those registered after provider selection. The bound prefix and connection settings are immutable; use a new container to change them.

`TagRetention` establishes a permanent scope minimum on first use. Later nodes may request at least that minimum; a shorter setting is rejected. Value deadlines remain capped by the established minimum, even when a later node requests longer retention. Use a new prefix to establish a different scope contract. Exact key removals retain tombstones for metadata retention across every entry format and policy identity. Writes use absolute physical deadlines anchored to source start, so slow serialization or transport cannot extend them.

Entry keys include the entry format and `SerializerVersion` (default 1); logical invalidation metadata does not. Raise the method `Version` or `DistributedCacheOptions.SerializerVersion` when changing result schemas or serializer settings. Content type only identifies the serialization family. Wire contract 1 frames key, application-tag, method and clear as separate operations. Unknown optional fields are ignored; incompatible mandatory frames retire local entries and produce one payload-free warning.

SQL Server creates only fresh schema contract 1 automatically. Existing unversioned or incompatible schema fails explicitly. The package includes `migrations/0001-version-existing-schema.sql`; stop all old nodes, back up the database and apply the supported migration before starting the new version. `CreateTablesIfMissing = false` prevents creation while retaining schema validation. `SqlServerOptions.ConnectionStringFactory` resolves once from DI.

Select JSON with `UseJson(options)` or `UseJson(context)`, or MessagePack with `UseMessagePack`. JSON options are copied and frozen. `DistributedCacheOptions.VerifyRoundTrip` defaults to true and can be disabled explicitly. The check cannot prove semantic equality: a nested derived value may lose fields during its first serialization without changing the outer runtime type or reserialized bytes. Configure polymorphic metadata/source-generated contexts when necessary. `WithDistributed(false)` skips method L2 reads and writes.

Redis and SQL Server own their backplane, enabled by default. If `EnableBackplane` is disabled, another instance can
keep an invalidated method result in L1 until it expires. HTTP storage reads shared generations before native L2
lookups and does not depend on backplane delivery. Disposing the service provider unsubscribes from the owned
backplane; a backplane that stalls delays its shutdown by at most twice `OperationTimeout`.

## Keep invalidations from being evicted

> [!WARNING]
> Tag, clear and key-removal stamps are ordinary expiring keys next to the entries they invalidate. A store that evicts a
> stamp under memory pressure while an entry it invalidated stays makes that entry valid again, on every instance, until
> it expires. Give the store room, and don't let it evict MethodCache's keys: for Redis, use `maxmemory-policy
> noeviction` (or a Redis of its own). Every MethodCache key has a time to live, so the `volatile-*` policies can evict
> them as well as the `allkeys-*` ones. With `noeviction`, a full Redis refuses writes instead: MethodCache then treats it
> as down and answers from memory. SQL Server removes rows only once they expired.

## Limits

- Invalidation matches exact keys and tags; common tags provide group invalidation.
- [Fail-safe](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/fail-safe.md) values and [runtime overrides](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/configuration.md#runtime-overrides) live in each instance's
  memory.

## Package guides

The [Redis](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/src/MethodCache.Redis/README.md) and [SQL Server](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/src/MethodCache.SqlServer/README.md) READMEs
cover their options, shared connections, table creation, outage settings and how each stores keys and invalidations.
The SQL Server guide also compares the two and has the schema migration for an existing invalidations table.

Caller cancellation stops the wait during an L2 read or a slow factory, including bulk reads and fail-safe waits. Shared work may finish for other callers; cancellation is not reported as a dependency failure.

SQL Server backplane initialization requires a non-nullable `binary(32)` `Scope` column. Incompatible scope columns
are reported without automatic schema upgrades; see the [SQL Server guide](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/src/MethodCache.SqlServer/README.md#required-backplane-schema).


---

<!-- source: docs/features/monitoring.md -->

# Monitoring

Core emits standard .NET metrics and activities. `AddMethodCache()` uses the container's `IMeterFactory`, registering
one when needed, and owns an `ActivitySource` with the same `MethodCacheTelemetry.Name` (`MethodCache`). Both use the
assembly version. Separate containers keep their observation callbacks separate.

## Administration and statistics

`ICacheAdministrator`, registered for the built-in manager, exposes local statistics, methods and entries:

```cs
var stats = await admin.GetStatsAsync();
var ratio = stats.Hits + stats.Misses == 0 ? 0 : (double)stats.Hits / (stats.Hits + stats.Misses);
Console.WriteLine($"Hit ratio {ratio:P0}, {stats.LocalMethodEntries} local method entries");
Console.WriteLine($"HTTP: {stats.LocalHttpEntries} local responses, {stats.LocalHttpBytes} stored bytes");
Console.WriteLine($"Method weight: {stats.TotalWeight} (configured weight units)");

foreach (var method in admin.GetMethods())
    Console.WriteLine($"{method.MethodId}: {method.Options.Duration}");

var entries = admin.ListEntries(tag: "user:42");
await admin.InvalidateTagsAsync(["user:42"]);
```

`Hits`, `Misses` and `Evictions` are local counters. Compute a hit ratio in the app or dashboard. Storage fields have
explicit scopes:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `LocalMethodEntries` | Method results resident in this instance |
| `LocalHttpEntries` | HTTP representations resident in this instance |
| `LocalHttpBytes` | HTTP storage cost in bytes; separate from method weight |
| `ObservedDistributedEntries` | Bounded HTTP observations, never a global L2 count |
| `TotalWeight` | Resident method weight in the configured weigher's units; one per entry without a weigher |

Statistics never serialize results or inspect their properties to estimate bytes. HTTP storage/observation fields
remain zero until the separate HTTP store is registered.

`GetMethods()` returns each method's `MethodId`, its effective `Options`, the `SettingSources` each setting comes from
and `IsDistributedNamespaceShared`. `ListEntries(storedKeyPrefix, tag, limit, methodId)` and `GetEntry(storedKey)`
inspect live local entries without values; listing is a diagnostic scan, not a transaction. `CacheEntryInfo.MethodId`
names the method an entry belongs to (`null` for manual entries and HTTP responses), and `ListEntries(methodId: ...)`
lists exactly that method's entries. `IMethodCacheKeys.MethodId` returns the id of a call ([Cache keys](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/keys.md)).
`CacheEntryInfo.StoredKey` is the key as stored, which `GetEntry` and `RemoveEntryAsync` take. For a manual entry with a
`Version` it includes the version, so it is not the key you pass to `ICacheManager`; there, use the key and version you
cached it with. `InvalidateMethodAsync(methodId)` removes every entry of one method, on every instance; an id no
cached method has throws an `ArgumentException`. `RemoveEntryAsync`, `InvalidateTagsAsync`, `InvalidateMethodAsync`
and `ClearAsync` complete once a configured distributed cache has confirmed the change, and throw
`CacheInvalidationQueuedException` when it is applied in memory but still queued for the distributed cache. Its
`Result` holds the counts of the invalidation (`null` for `ClearAsync`). The cache retries on its own; don't repeat
the call. `GetInvalidationQueues()` reports `Queued` (waiting for the distributed cache) and `PublicationQueued`
(waiting for the backplane). A custom or NoOp manager has no built-in method administrator or fabricated storage
statistics; with `AddHttpCaching` there is one for HTTP responses only.

## Admin endpoints

The `MethodCache.AspNetCore` package exposes administration behind an explicit authorization policy:

```cs
builder.Services.AddScoped<IUserService, UserService>();
builder.Services.AddMethodCache();
builder.Services.AddHealthChecks().AddMethodCache();
builder.Services.AddAuthorization(o => o.AddPolicy("CacheAdmins", p => p.RequireRole("Admin")));

var app = builder.Build();
app.UseAuthentication();
app.UseAuthorization();

app.MapMethodCacheAdmin("CacheAdmins");
app.MapHealthChecks("/health");
```

The [package README](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/src/MethodCache.AspNetCore/README.md#endpoints) lists the endpoints. Policies are read-only;
use [runtime overrides](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/configuration.md#runtime-overrides) to change them.

Configure your application's authentication scheme as well as the authorization policy. The
[web demo](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/samples/MethodCache.WebDemo) uses cookies and returns 401 for anonymous admin requests and
403 for signed-in callers without the `Admin` role outside Development. It has no sign-in page; its
Development environment allows anonymous admin requests so you can try the endpoints locally.
It also exposes Development-only `/demo/queries` and `/demo/reset` routes to count source reads and restore
the demonstration data; those routes are not part of the MethodCache admin package.
The sample price endpoint rejects missing, null and negative prices before writes or invalidation; rejected requests
leave both stored products and the cache unchanged.

## Health check

`AddHealthChecks().AddMethodCache()` reports the selected `failureStatus` (default `Degraded`) when L2 is unavailable,
either recovery queue has work, or a configured backplane is unknown, connecting or disconnected. A successful L2
probe does not prove that invalidation subscription is established. Reports include `managerCapability`,
`statisticsAvailable`, `distributedCacheAvailable` when applicable, `backplaneStatus`, `queued` and
`publicationQueued`, plus local storage statistics; the
[package README](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/src/MethodCache.AspNetCore/README.md#health-check) lists every key. Backend exception text is
omitted.

An incompatible distributed schema or retention contract reports `Unhealthy` with an actionable safe reason,
uses local memory only, and retains invalidations. A safe established retention differing from the configured
value reports `Degraded`. Admin mutations return 503 when distributed storage has not confirmed invalidation;
the cache continues owning retries.

An empty queue and a connected subscription do not acknowledge delivery to every node; backplane delivery remains
best effort.

## OpenTelemetry

The optional `MethodCache.OpenTelemetry` package provides `AddMethodCacheInstrumentation()` on meter and tracer
builders. These extensions only subscribe to Core's instruments; they do not wrap, replace or take ownership of your
manager. SDK setup may precede or follow `AddMethodCache()`, and repeated subscriptions do not multiply events.

```cs
builder.Services.AddMethodCache();

builder.Services.AddOpenTelemetry()
    .WithTracing(tracing => tracing
        .AddAspNetCoreInstrumentation()
        .AddMethodCacheInstrumentation()
        .AddOtlpExporter())
    .WithMetrics(metrics => metrics
        .AddMethodCacheInstrumentation()
        .AddOtlpExporter());
```

Each completed cache call has one `methodcache.requests` outcome, `methodcache.result`: `hit`, `miss`, `stale`,
`revalidated`, `bypass` or `error`. `methodcache.kind` is `method`, `manual` or `http`, and `methodcache.method` (a
method id) or `methodcache.http.client` (a client name) says which; manual calls by key carry neither. Every attribute
is in the `methodcache.` namespace, apart from `error.type`. A failed fast probe is not a separate miss.
Refreshes record their actual origin duration without another user request. Flight joiners and L2 hits do not record
origin loads. A bulk call has one outcome and measures its actual batch factory, rather than the per-key publication
of the already produced values.

Histograms use seconds, with bucket boundaries from 5 ms to 10 s. Local entry/HTTP byte instruments are observable
up-down counters. Invalidation counters count
distinct targets at each stage, not operation totals; do not add stages together. See the
[full instrument table](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/src/MethodCache.OpenTelemetry/README.md#metrics).

Spans cover actual origin loads, individual distributed operations and invalidation. Pure hits have no spans. Keys
and tags require explicit Core options; keys are hashed by default when enabled. Metrics never include keys, tags,
URLs, user ids or tenant ids. The library adds no baggage and copies no request HTTP/URL attributes. Normal ambient
.NET activity context and application-owned baggage continue to flow; configure their export in the app.

## Standard .NET listeners

OpenTelemetry is optional. A `MeterListener` can subscribe directly; retain it for the measurement lifetime:

```cs
builder.Services.AddMethodCache();
using var listener = new MeterListener();
listener.InstrumentPublished = (instrument, active) =>
{
    if (instrument.Meter.Name == MethodCacheTelemetry.Name)
        active.EnableMeasurementEvents(instrument);
};
listener.SetMeasurementEventCallback<long>((instrument, value, _, _) =>
    Console.WriteLine($"{instrument.Name}: {value}"));
listener.Start(); // keep the listener alive for as long as measurements are needed
```

Identity options belong to Core and do not depend on an exporter:

```cs
// Core emits standard Meter and ActivitySource instruments
builder.Services.AddMethodCache(mc => mc.Telemetry(options =>
{
    options.RecordCacheKeys = false;
    options.RecordCacheTags = false;
}));
```

For generated calls through a custom manager, Core can observe whether its supplied factory ran. Standalone calls to
an application-owned manager must be instrumented by that implementation; its storage capabilities are not assumed.


---

<!-- source: docs/features/memory-cache.md -->

# Memory cache

The in-memory cache uses W-TinyLFU eviction: when it is full, it keeps the entries that are read often and
evicts the rest, so a burst of one-off reads doesn't push out your hot data. Configure it with
`mc.Memory(o => ...)`, which sets `MethodCacheMemoryOptions`:

```cs
builder.Services.AddMethodCache(cache => cache
    .Defaults(o => o.WithDuration(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(10)))
    .Memory(o =>
    {
        o.MaxItems = 50_000;                              // default 10,000
        o.JitterMaxDuration = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30);   // spread out entries created together
        o.CacheNullValues = false;                        // a null result means "try again next time"
    }));
```

| Option | Default | What it does |
|--------|---------|--------------|
| `MaxItems` | 10,000 | The most entries kept, also when a `Weigher` is set |
| `WeightLimit` | 1000 MB | The most total weight kept; needs a `Weigher` |
| `Weigher` | none | Returns an entry's cost, for example its size in bytes |
| `MaxExpiration` | 7 days | No entry lives longer, whatever its duration |
| `JitterMaxDuration` | zero | Adds a random extra lifetime up to this value, so entries created together don't expire together |
| `CacheNullValues` | `true` | Caches `null` results like any other value |
| `MaxHttpBytes` | 100 MiB | The most bytes the HTTP response cache keeps in memory, bodies and headers included. Shared by all HTTP clients and separate from `MaxItems` and `WeightLimit` |

Method defaults are set with `Defaults.WithDuration`; unset defaults use five minutes. Cleanup, statistics and
the generated fast path are always enabled.

## How a call is answered

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A([Call a cached method]):::dark --> B{In memory?}
    B -- yes --> R([Return the same instance]):::amber
    B -- no --> C[Concurrent callers with the<br/>same key share one call]:::light
    C --> E[Run your method]:::dark
    E -- returns --> F[Store it, unless CacheWhen<br/>or CacheNullValues rejects it]:::light --> R
    E -- throws --> X(["Nothing is stored: the caller gets<br/>the exception or a fail-safe value"]):::dark
    classDef dark fill:#1E1B3A,stroke:#1E1B3A,color:#F5F3FF
    classDef amber fill:#FFB020,stroke:#FFB020,color:#1E1B3A
    classDef light fill:#F5F3FF,stroke:#1E1B3A,color:#1E1B3A
```

## Bounding by size

Object sizes can't be measured reliably at runtime, so to bound the cache by memory you say what an entry costs:

```cs
builder.Services.AddMethodCache(cache => cache.Memory(o =>
{
    o.WeightLimit = 256 * 1024 * 1024;   // bound the cache by total size as well as by count
    o.Weigher = (key, value) => value is string s ? s.Length * 2 : 64;
}));
```

The weigher must be fast, thread-safe and return a non-negative value. Both limits apply: an entry is evicted as soon
as either `MaxItems` or `WeightLimit` is reached, so raise `MaxItems` too when many small entries should fit. Setting
`WeightLimit` without a `Weigher` fails at startup, since there is nothing to weigh entries with.

## Memory statistics

`GetStatsAsync().TotalWeight` reports the resident method weight in the configured weigher's units. Without a
weigher, every method entry weighs one; a large returned object does not turn this field into bytes.
`LocalMethodEntries` reports the actual local entry count. Statistics never serialize results or inspect user
properties, and there are no sampling/accurate-estimation modes. HTTP entries and bytes use separate fields and budgets.

## How strict the bound is

Cache hits never wait for eviction. It runs in batches off the read path, so a new entry is stored at once and counted
against `MaxItems` and `WeightLimit` when the next batch applies it. Under any load:

- The counted size or weight is never more than one entry over the bound.
- When writers get ahead of eviction, they wait for it and help with it, so at most `16 × processor count` (at least
  64) inserts, plus two per writing thread, are stored but not yet counted.

Moments after the writes stop, the cache is back within the bound.

## Null values

`null` results are cached by default, so a method that returns `null` isn't run again on every call. Set
`CacheNullValues = false` when `null` means "not there yet" and the next call should try again, or use
[`CacheWhen`](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/conditional-caching.md) for one method.

## Cached objects are shared

> [!WARNING]
> The cache stores the object your method returned and hands the same instance to every caller. Don't change a cached
> object; return immutable types such as records, or copies.

Weighted capacity accounting remains nonnegative even for valid weights near `long.MaxValue`. Before an addition could overflow, the engine evicts existing weight; normal capacity/admission behavior is unchanged below that arithmetic limit.

Dictionary hashes are process-local implementation metadata. Canonical key text, L2 identities, administration and
invalidation remain stable across processes and restarts; the lookup hash is never stored or transmitted.


---

<!-- source: docs/features/native-aot.md -->

# Native AOT

MethodCache works in Native AOT and trimmed applications when your cached methods take arguments the decorator can
write into the key itself (see [Keys](#keys) below). The source generator writes the decorators, their registration
and those keys at build time. CI publishes a test application with Native AOT on every change and checks that
caching (with simple, record, collection and `ICacheKeyProvider` arguments), explicit `AutoRegister(ServiceLifetime)` registration and
`[assembly: CacheInterface]` work.

CI also compiles the complete supported signature corpus with Native AOT. This checks generated signatures and
ref safety across all key forms; reflection-based fallback cases retain the runtime limitations described below.

## In-memory caching

Nothing to do: the in-memory cache stores your objects as they are, without serializing them.

## Distributed caching

Values written to Redis or SQL Server are serialized with System.Text.Json. Under Native AOT it needs a
`JsonSerializerContext` that lists every type your cached methods return:

```cs
[JsonSerializable(typeof(Product))]
[JsonSerializable(typeof(List<Product>))]   // every type a cached method returns
public sealed partial class ShopJsonContext : JsonSerializerContext;
```

```cs
builder.Services.AddMethodCache(mc => mc
    .UseRedis("localhost:6379")
    .UseJson(ShopJsonContext.Default));
```

Select your context with `MethodCacheBuilder.UseJson(context)`. MethodCache cannot generate this context
for you, because one source generator can't see another generator's output.

## Keys

Under Native AOT, give cached methods arguments that the decorator writes into the key itself:

- simple values (strings, numbers, `bool`, `Guid`, dates, enums),
- records, classes and structs whose public properties and fields are simple values, passed as exactly the declared
  type (a sealed type is safest: an instance of a derived class goes through the key generator),
- types that implement `ICacheKeyProvider`,
- arrays, lists and sets of those (records and classes in them must be sealed), and dictionaries whose keys and values
  are simple values.

Collection subclasses with their own public state also use the key generator; implement `ICacheKeyProvider` on
these types when using Native AOT. Plain lists, arrays and sets keep their inline keys.

Other arguments, such as interfaces, `object` or collections of collections, go through the key generator, which
serializes them with reflection-based System.Text.Json. Publishing then reports trim and AOT warnings (IL2026,
IL3050) from `MethodCache.Core`, and the call throws `InvalidOperationException` at runtime. Wrap such an argument in a type that
implements `ICacheKeyProvider`, as `TenantId` does in [Cache keys](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/keys.md#types-whose-state-is-private).


---

<!-- source: docs/features/testing.md -->

# Testing

The implementation of a cached interface is a plain class: create it directly in unit tests and no caching is
involved.

## Testing with caching

To test the caching itself, such as invalidation tags, build a service provider the way the application does:

```cs
var services = new ServiceCollection();
services.AddSingleton<Database>();
services.AddScoped<IProductService, ProductService>();
services.AddMethodCache();
var provider = services.BuildServiceProvider();

// Resolved through the generated decorator, exactly as in the application
var products = provider.CreateScope().ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<IProductService>();
```

`ICacheAdministrator` from the same provider lists the entries and their keys, which helps when a test needs to check
what was cached ([Monitoring](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/monitoring.md)).

## Turning method caching off

Register `NoOpCacheManager` after `AddMethodCache()` and every call reaches your implementation:

```cs
var services = new ServiceCollection();
services.AddSingleton<Database>();
services.AddScoped<IProductService, ProductService>();
services.AddMethodCache();
services.AddSingleton<ICacheManager, NoOpCacheManager>();   // after AddMethodCache: every call reaches ProductService
```

For code that uses [manual caching](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/manual-caching.md), pass a `NoOpCacheManager` directly, or mock the four
operations on `ICacheManager`. The options-builder convenience overload delegates to that interface contract:

```cs
ICacheManager cache = new NoOpCacheManager();   // never caches: the factory runs on every call
var reader = new OrderReader(cache, repository);
```

`NoOpCacheManager` is in the `MethodCache` namespace and sealed. It disables method caching; HTTP response storage remains
independent. Configure HTTP caching separately and use its administrator for invalidation.

## Time

> [!TIP]
> The cache reads the time from the `TimeProvider` registered in the container, if there is one. Register a fake
> `TimeProvider`, for example from `Microsoft.Extensions.TimeProvider.Testing`, to test expiration without waiting.
> This includes the background cleanup of the memory cache and, with `MethodCache.HttpCaching`, response freshness,
> eviction and the background revalidation timeout.

The web demo uses a shared SQLite database in the temp folder (`methodcache-webdemo-products.db`), so concurrent price updates from either demo instance are atomic. Decimal prices retain full precision. The earlier temporary JSON file is left untouched; the SQLite catalog starts with the demo seed data.


---

<!-- source: docs/security.md -->

# Security

What each package protects against, what it leaves to you, and the tests that hold it to that.

## Self-hosted CI pilot

The opt-in Actions pilot uses a dedicated Nimbus account and a restricted organization runner group.
MethodCache is public: neither the caller nor the reusable workflow permits pull-request events. Only
trusted pushes/manual dispatches on the reviewed main/bootstrap branches can reach the job; checkout
uses that event's commit, with read-only token permissions and credential persistence disabled.
The external `MethodCache CI` merge gate remains independent.

The account's Docker access is root-equivalent. A separate account is not a sandbox, and runner groups
and event guards do not protect against a malicious repository writer. Do not add untrusted forks,
production secrets or signing credentials. Disposable execution isolation is required before widening
that trust boundary. The host capacity lease prevents overlapping heavy CI, not hostile code execution.
`build/ci/tests/test_actions_linux.py` verifies admission, lease lifetime, missing-lock refusal, and
failure/timeout propagation; the workflow event/ref gates are part of security review.

## Release publishing

`build/ci/publish.sh <tag>` retrieves only the configured BWS publishing secret after packing. The
NuGet API key goes to a .NET SDK 10.0.300+ CLI through `NUGET_API_KEY` and `NUGET_SYMBOL_API_KEY`, without appearing in command-line
arguments or shell traces. The BWS token is removed from the upload process's environment; inherited BWS
and both NuGet publishing credentials are removed from build-step environments. The script refuses a release
whose `MethodCache CI` status is not green. `build/ci/tests/test_publish.py` covers these boundaries and
failure paths. The host, release code and SDK remain trusted: this does not isolate malicious code running
under the same OS user from local credential files.

## MethodCache (keys, tags, invalidation)

| Threat | What MethodCache does |
|---|---|
| A caller crafts an argument (`"1:orders"`, `"a)"`, a newline) so that their call gets another call's key and its cached result | Keys separate arguments unambiguously: string parts escape `\` and `:`, `null` is `\0`, records are `(a:b)` with escaped members, and hashed keys length-prefix every value and record the runtime type of values in `object`, base-class or interface slots (`1` and `1L` in an `object[]` differ). JSON and MessagePack key-provider parts and nested strings preserve exact UTF-16 code units, including lone surrogates. Recursive key generation from providers or JSON getters cannot overwrite another invocation's key arguments. Arguments whose only state is private, including fields inherited from base classes, are rejected rather than hashed as an empty object. Framework types are written by their value (`BigInteger`, `IPAddress`, `JsonElement` and the others in [Cache keys](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/keys.md#framework-types)), not by public properties such as `BigInteger.Sign`, and any other type from .NET, ASP.NET Core or Microsoft.Extensions in a key, such as `StringBuilder`, is build error MC0019. Overloaded methods include the namespaces of their parameter types, so equally named types from different namespaces cannot share a method identity, and a method name that two interfaces of one hierarchy declare adds the parameter types (and the declaring interface for equal signatures) to the key, so `ILookup.Find(int)` and `ICatalog.Find(string)` cannot share an entry through the `ICatalog` decorator. Collection subclasses include their own public state alongside their elements in every key generator. No argument list produces another method's key or another argument list's key. Fluent versions have a separate namespace, with reserved user-key prefixes escaped, so a crafted raw key cannot reach a versioned entry. |
| Two service libraries declare identical namespace/type names | Generated service keys and policy ids include the assembly simple name, without its version; keyed-service enum types, closed generic arguments and fallback runtime types (including nested object values) also include assembly identity. Assembly-name delimiters are escaped. `AssemblyKeySecurityTests` and the cross-assembly SignatureCorpus regression verify separate values and overrides. Libraries with the same assembly identity are trusted as the same logical library; this is not isolation between AssemblyLoadContexts. |
| An argument that is a secret ends up readable | Keys contain argument values in plain text (hashed keys are not encryption) and appear in the admin endpoints and, if you turn them on, in traces. Don't cache methods that take passwords or tokens; pass an id. |
| A dynamic tag argument impersonates another argument | Dynamic placeholders use canonical key parts: null has its own marker, strings escape colons and backslashes, enums use invariant numbers, and dates keep their full precision. Static template text stays literal. Tags remain an application-defined shared invalidation namespace; they are not an authorization boundary. |
| A load races invalidation and a newer write | Invalidated loads cannot publish over newer entries, even when custom weight calculation stalls or re-enters the cache. Existing callers may finish with their pre-invalidation result; later loads and writes retain their own entry. |
| A tag built from user text clears the whole distributed cache | L2 metadata preserves every UTF-16 code unit, including lone surrogates, so reading a tag cannot change its invalidation identity. A tag is only ever its own tag, whatever characters it holds; the internal "clear everything" marker can't be named by a tag. |
| `*` or `?` in user text widens an invalidation | `InvalidateTagsAsync`, `InvalidateKeysAsync` and admin endpoints match exact keys and tags. Group invalidation uses an explicit common tag. |
| A tenant ID is missing from the cache key or invalidation scope | The console tenant example passes an explicit `Guid` tenant ID in the method arguments and tag, and `DemoTenantSecurityTests` verifies distinct results and selective invalidation. Applications must derive and authorize that tenant from the caller's identity. |

## Distributed cache (Redis, SQL Server)

| Threat | What MethodCache does |
|---|---|
| Corrupt, truncated or crafted bytes in the distributed cache | Read as a miss and loaded again: never an exception for the caller, never a `null` that wasn't stored, and lengths in the data are checked against its size before anything is allocated. |
| Stored data names a type to create (deserialization gadgets) | `JsonCacheSerializer` reads the method's declared type and ignores `$type`. `MessagePackCacheSerializer` uses the contractless resolver with `MessagePackSecurity.UntrustedData` and refuses typeless payloads. Keep it that way if you pass your own options. |
| Someone who can write to Redis or SQL Server | **Not prevented.** They can store any well-formed value, which every instance will serve. Owned Redis and SQL Server providers use backend-atomic maximum stamps and permanent epoch updates; their internal contracts are not application extension points. The distributed cache is trusted: protect it like your database (authentication, TLS, network rules), and give each application its own `KeyPrefix`. Redis uses injective escaping before UTF-8 encoding, including for atomic stamps, so different UTF-16 keys cannot alias through replacement characters. SQL Server hashes exact UTF-16 cache keys so collation cannot alias distinct data or invalidation metadata keys, including NULs and trailing spaces. SQL Server also scopes backplane messages and cleanup by that exact prefix, independently of database collation. Automatic initialization rejects missing, nullable or incorrectly typed scope columns; it requires `binary(32) NOT NULL`. |
| Invalidations evicted from the store | A store that evicts a tag or removal stamp under memory pressure makes the entries it invalidated valid again (for example data cached before a permission change). Run Redis with `maxmemory-policy noeviction` or a Redis of its own; see [Keep invalidations from being evicted](https://github.com/eoniclabs/MethodCache/blob/main/docs/features/distributed-cache.md#keep-invalidations-from-being-evicted). |
| Backplane messages | Carry keys and tags in lossless UTF-16 frames, so lone surrogates cannot change invalidation identity and newlines cannot forge another message type. Messages from another MethodCache version are rejected with one warning, without logging their contents. Anyone who can publish on the channel can invalidate entries, so the same trust applies. |

## MethodCache.AspNetCore (admin endpoints)

| Threat | What MethodCache does |
|---|---|
| An endpoint reachable without authorization | `MapMethodCacheAdmin` requires an authorization policy name, and every endpoint it maps requires that policy: anonymous callers get 401, signed-in users without it 403. A test reads the app's route table and checks every mapped endpoint, so a new endpoint without the policy fails a test. |
| The web demo is started outside Development | It requires cookie authentication and the `Admin` role, returning 401/403 for refused requests. Only Development permits anonymous admin access. `WebDemoSecurityTests` starts the actual sample and checks every admin route in both environments. The sample has no sign-in page; deployed applications must configure their own authentication. |
| Demo data can be reset outside Development | `/demo/reset` and `/demo/queries` are mapped only in Development. The sample tests verify that Production returns 404 for both. |
| A web demo price update omits a price or supplies null/negative input | The endpoint returns 400 before writing or invalidating. `WebDemoInputTests` verifies stored and cached products stay unchanged, and checks zero and the maximum decimal as valid boundaries. |
| A cross-site form or `fetch` without preflight calls `invalidate`, `invalidate-method` or `clear` with the admin's cookie | The `POST` endpoints only accept an `application/json` body, which a browser sends cross-site only after a CORS preflight; forms and `text/plain` get 415, and a request without a body 400. `DELETE entry` needs a preflight too. Don't add a CORS policy that allows these routes from other origins. |
| A filter in the wrong place empties the whole cache | Emptying everything is its own endpoint, `POST clear`, which takes only `{}`: a body with any property, such as `{ "tags": [...] }`, is 400. `invalidate` takes only `tags` and `invalidate-method` only `methodId`, and an unknown query parameter is 400 on every endpoint, so a misplaced filter is rejected instead of ignored. |
| `invalidate-method` removes another method's entries | The `methodId` must be exactly the id of a cached method, as `methods` lists it; anything else is 400 and removes nothing. Entries are matched by the method they belong to, not by a key prefix, so `GetUser` never reaches `GetUsers`. |
| Cached values leak through the admin API | Entries are listed with stored key, method id, value type, age, time to live, tags and size, never the value. Keys contain argument values (see above), so the policy should admit only operators. |
| Bad input | A missing `storedKey` or `methodId`, a `methodId` no cached method has, or an out-of-range `limit` is 400, an empty or blank tag list is 400, and keys, tags and method ids are matched literally, never as patterns. |

The health check reports counts only. If you map it with a detailed response writer, put that endpoint behind
authorization too.

## MethodCache.HttpCaching

| Threat | What MethodCache does |
|---|---|
| Two users of one `HttpClient` get each other's responses (private cache, the default) | `Authorization` and `Cookie` are part of every response's key, including values that don't parse as a credential, so each caller only gets responses fetched with their own headers. `AddHttpCaching()` disables automatic cookies on known transports after all handler configuration; `KeepCookies=true` preserves the transport and bypasses response caching, validation and stale fallback completely; explicitly supplied cookie headers isolate callers. Unknown transports, and handlers inside the primary transport, bypass caching unless explicitly verified and opted in with `AllowUnverifiedTransport`. A directly constructed cache handler also bypasses known transports with automatic cookies enabled. An empty header and no header are different callers too. Header values are individually length-framed as exact UTF-16, so a comma cannot alias multiple values and isolated surrogates cannot collapse through replacement encoding. |
| A 200 or 304 changes response privacy or variant selection | Revalidated representations are checked again: `no-store`, `Vary: *` or shared-cache `private` removes previous responses. An omitted `Vary` on a 304 keeps its previous value. Unstorable full replacements also retire the old body, and selection-rule changes retire its URL epoch once so a newer concurrent publication remains reachable, including when old-entry deletion fails after a successful rotation. |
| A shared cache (`IsSharedCache = true`) stores a personal response | Responses marked `private`, and responses to requests with any `Authorization` header, are not stored unless they say `public`, `s-maxage` or `must-revalidate` (RFC 9111 section 3.5). |
| Stale content bypasses required validation | Response or request `no-cache` requires successful validation even with stale-while-revalidate or stale-if-error enabled; origin failures propagate. |
| A cached response hands out a session | `Set-Cookie` is never stored. The caller the origin answered gets it, including on a `304`; nobody answered from the cache does. |
| Responses that vary by a header (tenant, language) get mixed | `Vary` and `KeyHeaders` keep one response per value. `Vary: *` is never served from the cache. |
| A write leaves another caller's stale copy, or serves one caller's copy to another after it | A confirmed `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH` or `DELETE` atomically advances every relevant shared URL generation before returning, including for bypass/KeepCookies clients. Older origin/304/body writes remain in an obsolete namespace. L2 nodes capture fresh generations in one bounded metadata batch; correctness does not rely on backplane delivery. An unconfirmed mutation throws `HttpCacheInvalidationException`, disposes its response and retains owned recovery after caller cancellation. The origin may have succeeded: do not automatically repeat it. A GET or HEAD whose answer replaces a stored response that can't be retired throws the same exception; it is safe to retry. |
| Two URLs share an entry | The key is the method and the full URL, with reserved characters kept escaped (`%2F`, `%3F` and `/`, `?` are different URLs). |
| A followed redirect hands one caller's response to another | The transport drops `Authorization` on a redirect and changes the URL on the same message. A response that ended at another URL or method is never stored under the URL that was requested, and entries are keyed on the request as the caller sent it, before the transport changed it. |
| A malformed `Cache-Control` hides `private` or `no-store` | A `Cache-Control` or `Vary` field the parser rejects, also next to a valid one, makes the response not storable instead of being ignored. |
| Clients that get caching from `ConfigureHttpClientDefaults` share entries | Each client's handler gets its own name, so clients (often one per tenant or API key) never read each other's entries. |
| Lost or replayed HTTP generation metadata | Native atomic revisions only advance; missing/overflowed metadata gets a fresh initialization id. Old values never regain their namespace. Global/client/static-tag components are shared with Core-only tag/clear writes, including across value formats. URL-slot collisions cause extra misses, never shared caller identity. The local reverse index follows the same bounded slots and removes every retired body from an invalidated slot. Native observations keep their separate per-URL index. |
| Administration becomes a body or credential leak, or a false global inventory | Core exposes only resident metadata or at most 1024 historical, expiring, body-free L2 observations. Ids are bounded hashes; no raw query, credentials or cookie headers enter the observations. `ObservedDistributed` explicitly does not confirm presence or global inventory. Unknown ids are NotFound. |
| An oversized response exhausts the local HTTP budget | Method and HTTP budgets evict independently. Body reads are bounded by response limits and remaining conservative HTTP cost; oversized responses remain available as streams and are not cached. |
| Crafted entries in the distributed HTTP cache | Read as a miss, with every length checked against the data. As above, whoever can write that cache can store any response. |

Not guaranteed, by design:

- In a **shared** cache, a response stored for an anonymous request is served to authorized requests for the same URL
  too, and responses that depend on cookies are shared unless the origin sends `Vary: Cookie` or `private`. That is
  what RFC 9111 specifies for a shared cache. Add `Cookie` or `Authorization` to `KeyHeaders` when your origin
  personalises without saying so.
- Anonymous callers of a private cache are one caller: they share responses.
- HTTP key hashing preserves complete UTF-16 header frames; temporary pooled buffers are cleared before reuse.
- HTTP cache diagnostics omit raw URLs, headers and exception payloads. Static configured client names remain visible.
  Application/transport instrumentation has its own logging configuration.

## MethodCache.OpenTelemetry

Core owns the `MethodCache` Meter/ActivitySource. The OpenTelemetry package only subscribes to them.

| Signal | Recorded by default | Opt-in |
|---|---|---|
| Spans | `methodcache.kind`, the static `methodcache.method` or `methodcache.http.client`, `methodcache.operation` or `methodcache.invalidation.type`, and `error.type`; no exception messages, stacks or copied HTTP/URL attributes | Core `MethodCacheTelemetryOptions.RecordCacheKeys` (SHA-256 by default, raw with `HashCacheKeys=false`); `RecordCacheTags` for application tags |
